claims.claim: Segregation Distorter in Drosophila acts postmeiotically to disable male gametes that do not inherit it.
claims.source: In fact, some of the best-known meiotic drivers, such as Segregation Distorter in Drosophila and the t haplotype in mouse (Lyon, 2003; Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012), act postmeiotically to disable male gametes (sperms) that do not inherit them.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Segregation Distorter.

claims.claim: The t haplotype in mouse acts postmeiotically to disable male gametes that do not inherit it.
claims.source: In fact, some of the best-known meiotic drivers, such as Segregation Distorter in Drosophila and the t haplotype in mouse (Lyon, 2003; Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012), act postmeiotically to disable male gametes (sperms) that do not inherit them.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on the t haplotype.

claims.claim: Fungal gamete killers (spore killers) have been found in several filamentous ascomycetes, most notably Neurospora and Podospora anserina.
claims.source: Fungal gamete killers, or spore killers, have been found in several filamentous ascomycetes, most notably Neurospora and Podospora anserina (Dalstra et al., 2003; Grognet et al., 2014; Hammond et al., 2012; Turner and Perkins, 1979).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research on fungal spore killers.

claims.claim: S. pombe natural isolates have pair-wise nucleotide differences of less than 1%.
claims.source: S. pombe natural isolates, which are nearly all haploids and have pair-wise nucleotide differences of less than 1% (Jeffares et al., 2015; Rhind et al., 2011), can readily mate with each other to form hybrid diploids, but the viability of spores derived from inter-isolate crosses is often below 5% and in many instances under 1% (Gutz and Doe, 1975; Kondrat''eva and Naumov, 2001; Naumov et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic studies of S. pombe natural isolates.

claims.claim: The viability of spores derived from S. pombe inter-isolate crosses is often below 5% and in many instances under 1%.
claims.source: S. pombe natural isolates, which are nearly all haploids and have pair-wise nucleotide differences of less than 1% (Jeffares et al., 2015; Rhind et al., 2011), can readily mate with each other to form hybrid diploids, but the viability of spores derived from inter-isolate crosses is often below 5% and in many instances under 1% (Gutz and Doe, 1975; Kondrat''eva and Naumov, 2001; Naumov et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies documenting hybrid sterility in S. pombe.

claims.claim: S. cerevisiae natural isolates have a similar level of nucleotide diversity to S. pombe but much better spore viability when inter-crossed.
claims.source: This is in stark contrast to Saccharomyces cerevisiae, whose natural isolates have a similar level of nucleotide diversity but much better spore viability when inter-crossed (Hou et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a comparative study.

claims.claim: One chromosomal rearrangement reduces spore viability at most by half.
claims.source: However, because one rearrangement reduces spore viability at most by half (Avelar et al., 2013; Hou et al., 2014), other factors are likely in play.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on the effects of chromosomal rearrangements on spore viability.

claims.claim: At least three spore killers contributed to hybrid sterility when the S. pombe laboratory strain was crossed to S. pombe var. kambucha.
claims.source: It was shown recently that when the S. pombe laboratory strain, which was isolated from French grape juice (Hu et al., 2015; Osterwalder, 1924), was crossed to a strain isolated from fermented tea (initially called Schizosaccharomyces kambucha [Singh and Klar, 2003], later renamed S. pombe var. kambucha [Rhind et al., 2011]), at least three spore killers contributed to hybrid sterility (Bomblies, 2014; Zanders et al., 2014), but the identities of the killer genes were unknown.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on hybrid sterility between these strains.

claims.claim: Introducing a 2.23 Mb pericentric inversion on chromosome I into the laboratory strain increased spore viability in crosses with CBS5557 from 14% to 22%.
claims.source: After introducing the same inversion into the laboratory strain (Hu et al., 2015), the viability of spores derived from the cross between the laboratory strain and CBS5557 increased from 14% to 22% (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: NGS-assisted bulk segregant analysis revealed that SNP alleles of the laboratory strain on chromosome III were markedly under-represented among viable progenies from the cross with CBS5557.
claims.source: To uncover the causes of the remaining sterility, we performed next-generation sequencing (NGS)-assisted bulk segregant analysis (Hu et al., 2015) and found that among the viable progenies from the cross, SNP alleles of the laboratory strain (reference alleles) on chromosome III were markedly under-represented (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: Figure 1A shows the reference allele frequency data demonstrating under-representation on chromosome III.

claims.claim: Two broad transmission distortion peaks were observed on chromosome III, suggesting at least two spore killer genes.
claims.source: Two broad transmission distortion peaks, one on the left arm (hereafter referred to as the left peak) and one on the right arm (hereafter referred to as the right peak), were observed, suggesting that there are at least two spore killer genes on chromosome III of CBS5557.
claims.evidence: Figure 1A shows two distinct peaks of transmission distortion on chromosome III.

claims.claim: Deletion of cw9 from the backcrossed-1 strain notably reduced segregation distortion.
claims.source: We deleted from the backcrossed-1 strain a wtf gene locating at the position of wtf9 in the reference genome but exhibiting a low sequence identity (42%) to wtf9 in the 5' portion (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and found that the deletion notably reduced the segregation distortion (right-side plot in Figure 1B), suggesting that this wtf gene, which we named cw9 (the nomenclature of wtf genes in the CBS5557 genome will be explained later in this paper), is a spore killer.
claims.evidence: Figure 1B shows bulk segregant analysis data demonstrating reduced transmission distortion upon cw9 deletion.

claims.claim: Removing cw27 from the backcrossed-2 strain completely abolished segregation distortion.
claims.source: Within the CBS5557 genomic segment in the backcrossed-2 strain, we found a wtf gene absent in the reference genome, possibly owing to a deletion event mediated by homologous recombination between LTRs (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3). Removing this wtf gene, which we named cw27, from the backcrossed-2 strain completely abolished segregation distortion (right-side plot in Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: Figure 1C shows bulk segregant analysis data demonstrating complete abolishment of transmission distortion upon cw27 deletion.

claims.claim: cw27 appears to have been lost in the laboratory strain through a deletion event mediated by homologous recombination between LTRs.
claims.source: Within the CBS5557 genomic segment in the backcrossed-2 strain, we found a wtf gene absent in the reference genome, possibly owing to a deletion event mediated by homologous recombination between LTRs (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3 show sequence analysis supporting LTR-mediated recombination as the mechanism of deletion.

claims.claim: Homozygous deletion of cw9 or cw27 in CBS5557 had no effect on spore viability.
claims.source: Homozygous deletion of cw9 or cw27 had no effect on spore viability (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Figure 2A shows tetrad analysis data demonstrating normal spore viability with homozygous deletions.

claims.claim: Heterozygous deletion of cw9 or cw27 in CBS5557 caused a significant reduction of spore viability.
claims.source: In contrast, heterozygous deletion of either cw9 or cw27 caused a significant reduction of spore viability, which resulted mainly from the death of spores carrying the deletion (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: Figure 2A and 2B show tetrad analysis data demonstrating reduced spore viability with heterozygous deletions, with deletion-carrying spores predominantly affected.

claims.claim: When cw9 and cw27 were both heterozygous in CBS5557, double deletion mutant spores suffered a particularly high level of death.
claims.source: When cw9 and cw27 were both in the heterozygous state, a more severe loss of spore viability was observed, with the double deletion mutant spores suffering a particularly high level of death (Figure 2A and B, and Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: Figure 2A and 2B show tetrad analysis data demonstrating severe spore viability loss when both killers are heterozygous.

claims.claim: In crosses of laboratory strains where only one parent harbored cw9 or cw27, spores not inheriting the killer suffered significant loss of viability regardless of genomic location.
claims.source: In crosses where only one of the parental strains harbored cw9 or cw27, spores inheriting the killer had normal viability, whereas spores not inheriting the killer suffered significant loss of viability, regardless of the genomic location of the killer (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Figure 3A shows tetrad analysis data from crosses with killers at different genomic locations (his3, lys1, leu1).

claims.claim: When both parental laboratory strains contained the same killer at the leu1 locus, spore viability was normal.
claims.source: When both parental strains contained the same killer, spore viability was normal.
claims.evidence: Figure 3B shows tetrad analysis data demonstrating normal spore viability when both parents have the same killer.

claims.claim: When one parental laboratory strain had cw9 and the other had cw27 at the leu1 locus, spores inheriting either killer experienced dramatic loss of viability.
claims.source: In contrast, when one parental strain had cw9 and the other parental strain had cw27, spores inheriting either cw9 or cw27 experienced a dramatic loss of viability.
claims.evidence: Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2 show tetrad analysis data demonstrating mutual killing between cw9 and cw27.

claims.claim: Killer-affected spores fail to undergo a proper maturation process.
claims.source: These data suggest that killer-affected spores fail to undergo a proper maturation process.
claims.evidence: Figure 3C shows electron microscopy images demonstrating that killer-affected spores at 18 hours retain visible organelles and lower electron density cytoplasm, unlike properly matured control spores.

claims.claim: At 18 hours after shift to sporulation medium, asci derived from cw27-containing cells often exhibited a 2:2 pattern of spore morphology.
claims.source: Interestingly, at the same time point, asci derived from the cw27-containing cells often exhibited a 2:2 pattern of spore morphology: two spores in an ascus looked like the matured spores in the control sample, whereas the other two spores exhibited cytoplasm with a lower electron density and visible organelles, an electron-lucent spore wall, and frequently a non-spherical shape.
claims.evidence: Figure 3C shows electron microscopy images demonstrating the 2:2 pattern of spore morphology.

claims.claim: cw9 and cw27 share a nearly identical 288-bp-long conserved_up sequence upstream of their predicted start codons.
claims.source: cw9 and cw27 are both flanked by solo LTRs, and upstream of their predicted start codons they share a nearly identical 288-bp-long sequence (hereafter referred to as the conserved_up sequence) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which is also conserved upstream of the coding sequences of many other wtf genes (Bowen et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1 shows sequence alignment demonstrating the conserved_up sequence.

claims.claim: The flanking LTRs of cw9 and cw27 are not important for spore killing.
claims.source: The Ta versions, which lack the LTRs, caused spore killing phenotypes similar to those caused by longer constructs containing the flanking LTRs, indicating that the LTRs are not important.
claims.evidence: Figure 4A shows tetrad analysis data demonstrating that Ta versions without LTRs retain killing activity.

claims.claim: The Tb versions of cw9 and cw27 partially lost the ability to protect killer-containing spores from being harmed.
claims.source: Interestingly, the Tb versions missing the sequence between the upstream LTR and the conserved_up sequence caused spores containing the killer to suffer a moderate viability loss, suggesting that these truncated killer genes partially lost the ability to protect killer-containing spores from being harmed.
claims.evidence: Figure 4A shows tetrad analysis data demonstrating reduced protection by Tb versions.

claims.claim: Removing the last 10 amino-acid-coding codons from the Tc versions (Td versions) greatly diminished spore killing.
claims.source: Removing from the Tc versions, the last 10 amino-acid-coding codons (Td versions) greatly diminished spore killing, whereas removing from the Tc versions the sequences upstream of the start codons (Te versions) resulted in more indiscriminate killing than that caused by the Tb versions.
claims.evidence: Figure 4A shows tetrad analysis data demonstrating that Td versions have greatly reduced killing activity.

claims.claim: Intact C termini are important for the killing activity of wtf killers.
claims.source: These results suggest that intact C termini are important for the killing activity, and the upstream sequences are important for the protecting activity.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the truncation analysis data showing that Td versions lacking the last 10 amino acids have greatly diminished killing activity.

claims.claim: The upstream sequences of wtf killers are important for the protecting activity.
claims.source: These results suggest that intact C termini are important for the killing activity, and the upstream sequences are important for the protecting activity.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the truncation analysis data showing that Tb and Te versions with altered upstream sequences have reduced protecting activity.

claims.claim: The Td versions of cw9 and cw27 can effectively protect spores harboring them from being killed by the respective Tc-version killers.
claims.source: To determine whether the Td versions, which are largely devoid of the killing activity, can still protect, we performed crosses in which a strain with a Td-version-containing plasmid integrated at the ars1 locus was crossed to a strain with a Tc-version-containing plasmid integrated at the leu1 locus, and found that the Td versions of both cw9 and cw27 can effectively protect spores harboring them from being killed by the respective Tc-version killers (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Figure 4B shows tetrad analysis data demonstrating effective protection by Td versions against Tc-version killers.

claims.claim: In the reference genome, there are 25 wtf genes at 20 locations.
claims.source: In the reference genome, there are 25 wtf genes at 20 locations (15 singletons and five tandem pairs) (Bowen et al., 2003) (Figure 5A and B).
claims.evidence: Figure 5A and B show the genomic locations and organization of wtf genes in the reference genome, supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: In the CBS5557 genome, there are 32 wtf genes at 23 locations.
claims.source: Using PacBio sequencing, we found that in the CBS5557 genome, these 20 locations are occupied by 29 wtf genes (12 singletons, seven pairs, and one triplet), with four locations containing an extra wtf gene compared to the reference genome (Figure 5A and B).
claims.evidence: Figure 5A shows that CBS5557 has 32 wtf genes total (29 at syntenic locations plus 3 at new locations: cw26, cw27, cw28).

claims.claim: cw26 and cw28 appeared to have been lost in the laboratory strain through LTR-mediated recombination.
claims.source: Like cw27, cw26 and cw28 also appeared to have been lost in the laboratory strain through LTR-mediated recombination (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that this is a common mode of wtf gene turnover.
claims.evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1 shows sequence analysis supporting LTR-mediated recombination as the mechanism of deletion for cw26 and cw28.

claims.claim: LTR-mediated recombination is a common mode of wtf gene turnover.
claims.source: Like cw27, cw26 and cw28 also appeared to have been lost in the laboratory strain through LTR-mediated recombination (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that this is a common mode of wtf gene turnover.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that three singleton wtf genes (cw26, cw27, cw28) all appear to have been lost through the same LTR-mediated mechanism.

claims.claim: Six CBS5557 singleton wtf genes exhibit exceptionally high DNA sequence diversity (<85% identity) from their counterparts in the reference genome.
claims.source: Among the 12 CBS5557 singleton wtf genes with syntenic counterparts in the reference genome, cw9 and five others exhibit exceptionally high DNA sequence diversity (<85% identity) from their counterparts in the reference genome (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 2 shows sequence identity data for syntenic wtf gene pairs.

claims.claim: wtf genes have diverged at a much faster pace than average genes.
claims.source: Given that the genome-wide nucleotide difference between CBS5557 and the laboratory strain is only 3.1 SNPs/kb (Hu et al., 2015), wtf genes must have diverged at a much faster pace than average genes.
claims.evidence: This is inferred by comparing the high sequence divergence of wtf genes (<85% identity for some) to the low genome-wide divergence (3.1 SNPs/kb).

claims.claim: Only 11 of 16 phylogenetic neighbor pairs conform to typical orthologous relationship where two members are syntenic.
claims.source: Interestingly, only 11 of these 16 pairs conform to typical orthologous relationship where two members of a pair are syntenic (highlighted by green rectangles in Figure 5C), whereas the five other pairs each consist of two genes that are non-syntenic (highlighted by yellow rectangles in Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: Figure 5C shows the phylogenetic tree with colored rectangles highlighting syntenic and non-syntenic phylogenetic neighbor pairs.

claims.claim: Ectopic gene conversion may contribute to the inter-isolate difference of wtf genes.
claims.source: This pattern suggests that ectopic gene conversion (also called non-allelic or interlocus gene conversion) may contribute to the inter-isolate difference of wtf genes (Chen et al., 2007; Petes and Hill, 1988).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic pattern showing non-syntenic genes as phylogenetic neighbors, supported by citations to literature on ectopic gene conversion.

claims.claim: Genes belonging to the same wtf gene cluster are very distinct from each other.
claims.source: Interestingly, genes belonging to the same gene cluster (pair or triplet), despite being subject more strongly to the homogenizing effect of gene conversion due to their physical proximity, are without exception very distinct from each other.
claims.evidence: This is observed from the phylogenetic tree in Figure 5C where clustered genes do not group together phylogenetically.

claims.claim: Diversifying selection may have prevented sequence homogenization within wtf gene clusters.
claims.source: One possible explanation is that diversifying selection may have prevented sequence homogenization within gene clusters.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed high divergence within gene clusters.

claims.claim: Segregation Distorter in Drosophila contains at least two key loci: a killer locus and a target locus.
claims.source: Two well-studied gamete killers in animals, Segregation Distorter in Drosophila and the t haplotype in mouse, both contain at least two key loci, a killer locus and a target locus (Lyon, 2003; Burt and Trivers, 2006; Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012; Lindholm et al., 2016; Bauer et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Segregation Distorter.

claims.claim: The t haplotype in mouse contains at least two key loci: a killer locus and a target locus.
claims.source: Two well-studied gamete killers in animals, Segregation Distorter in Drosophila and the t haplotype in mouse, both contain at least two key loci, a killer locus and a target locus (Lyon, 2003; Burt and Trivers, 2006; Larracuente and Presgraves, 2012; Lindholm et al., 2016; Bauer et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on the t haplotype.

claims.claim: Spore killers of Neurospora appear to comprise two genes: rsk and a yet-to-be-identified killer gene.
claims.source: In fungi, spore killers of Neurospora also appear to comprise of two genes, rsk (resistant to Spore killer) and a yet-to-be-identified killer gene, which are proposed to act together in a fashion similar to the toxin-antitoxin (TA) systems of bacterial plasmids, in which a stable toxin and a labile antitoxin together ensure that bacterial cells cannot lose the plasmid expressing them (Hammond et al., 2012; McLaughlin and Malik, 2017; Saupe, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Neurospora spore killers.

claims.claim: Two types of single-gene spore killers, [Het-s] prion and the Spok genes, have been found in Podospora anserina.
claims.source: On the other hand, two types of single-gene spore killers, [Het-s] prion and the Spok genes, have been found in the filamentous fungus Podospora anserina (Dalstra et al., 2003; Grognet et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Podospora anserina spore killers.

claims.claim: The killing activity of the [Het-s] prion requires the presence of the HET-S protein.
claims.source: The killing activity of the [Het-s] prion requires the presence of the HET-S protein, whereas the Spok genes can act autonomously.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the [Het-s] prion system.

claims.claim: Spok genes can act autonomously.
claims.source: The killing activity of the [Het-s] prion requires the presence of the HET-S protein, whereas the Spok genes can act autonomously.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Spok genes.

claims.claim: wtf killers share two prominent features with Spok killers: being composed of a single predicted coding sequence and acting in a self-sufficient manner.
claims.source: Fission yeast wtf killers share two prominent features with the Spok killers: being composed of a single predicted coding sequence and acting in a self-sufficient manner.
claims.evidence: This is based on the structural and functional characterization of wtf killers presented in the manuscript and comparison to published work on Spok killers.

claims.claim: wtf genes only exist in S. pombe.
claims.source: Firstly, wtf genes only exist in a single fission yeast species S. pombe, indicating that they probably have arisen after the divergence of S. pombe from its closest relatives S. octosporus and S. cryophilus around 120 million years ago (Rhind et al., 2011), and have not jumped across the species barriers.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to comparative genomic studies and the absence of wtf homologs in other species.

claims.claim: wtf genes probably arose after the divergence of S. pombe from S. octosporus and S. cryophilus around 120 million years ago.
claims.source: Firstly, wtf genes only exist in a single fission yeast species S. pombe, indicating that they probably have arisen after the divergence of S. pombe from its closest relatives S. octosporus and S. cryophilus around 120 million years ago (Rhind et al., 2011), and have not jumped across the species barriers.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the species-specific distribution of wtf genes and citation to phylogenetic studies.

claims.claim: Spok family genes have a patchy but widespread distribution among Pezizomycotina species.
claims.source: In contrast, Spok family genes have a patchy but widespread distribution among Pezizomycotina species (Grognet et al., 2014), whose last common ancestor dates to 400 million years ago (Prieto and Wedin, 2013), suggesting that Spok killers have originated much earlier than wtf killers or have been especially prone to transfer horizontally across species.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Spok gene distribution.

claims.claim: spok family genes encode soluble proteins with a C-terminal kinase-like domain.
claims.source: Secondly, spok family genes encode soluble proteins with a C-terminal kinase-like domain (InterPro:IPR011009), whereas wtf genes are predicted to encode multi-transmembrane proteins, suggesting that the detailed molecular mechanisms of these two types of killers are likely to be quite distinct.
claims.evidence: This is based on protein domain analysis and established knowledge about Spok proteins.

claims.claim: wtf genes are predicted to encode multi-transmembrane proteins.
claims.source: Secondly, spok family genes encode soluble proteins with a C-terminal kinase-like domain (InterPro:IPR011009), whereas wtf genes are predicted to encode multi-transmembrane proteins, suggesting that the detailed molecular mechanisms of these two types of killers are likely to be quite distinct.
claims.evidence: This is based on computational prediction of protein structure shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4 and 5.

claims.claim: Nuckolls et al. showed that the wtf4 gene from S. pombe var. kambucha acts as a spore killer by expressing two overlapping transcripts.
claims.source: Consistent with this idea, Nuckolls et al. showed that the wtf4 gene from the S. pombe var. kambucha strain (Sk wtf4) acts as a spore killer by expressing two overlapping transcripts, with the shorter transcript encoding a spore-killing poison and the longer transcript encoding an antidote that protects the spores from the killing effect of the poison (Nuckolls et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to the Nuckolls et al. study.

claims.claim: In the wtf4 dual-transcript model, the shorter transcript encodes a spore-killing poison and the longer transcript encodes an antidote.
claims.source: Consistent with this idea, Nuckolls et al. showed that the wtf4 gene from the S. pombe var. kambucha strain (Sk wtf4) acts as a spore killer by expressing two overlapping transcripts, with the shorter transcript encoding a spore-killing poison and the longer transcript encoding an antidote that protects the spores from the killing effect of the poison (Nuckolls et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to the Nuckolls et al. study.

claims.claim: cw9, cw27, and 10 other wtf genes share a 150 bp conserved sequence in the predicted intron 1.
claims.source: Indeed, through inspecting the DNA sequence alignment (Figure 5—source data 1), we found that cw9, cw27, and 10 other wtf genes in the reference genome and the CBS5557 genome share a 150 bp conserved sequence in the predicted intron 1, and this sequence is closely upstream of the transcription start site of a shorter-than-predicted wtf23 transcript isoform uncovered by the Iso-Seq long-read RNA sequencing method (Figure 5—figure supplement 3) (Kuang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 3 shows the alignment of the 150 bp conserved sequence and its relationship to the wtf23 transcript start site.

claims.claim: The 150 bp conserved sequence is closely upstream of the transcription start site of a shorter wtf23 transcript isoform.
claims.source: Indeed, through inspecting the DNA sequence alignment (Figure 5—source data 1), we found that cw9, cw27, and 10 other wtf genes in the reference genome and the CBS5557 genome share a 150 bp conserved sequence in the predicted intron 1, and this sequence is closely upstream of the transcription start site of a shorter-than-predicted wtf23 transcript isoform uncovered by the Iso-Seq long-read RNA sequencing method (Figure 5—figure supplement 3) (Kuang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Iso-Seq data and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The 12 genes containing the 150 bp sequence can be classified into Intron-1-ATG genes and Exon-2-ATG genes based on the locations of the first ATG codons downstream of the 150 bp sequence.
claims.source: These 12 genes can be classified into two subtypes, which we call Intron-1-ATG genes (wtf4, wtf13, cw4, cw18, and cw23) and Exon-2-ATG genes (wtf19, wtf23, cw8a, cw9, cw21, cw22, and cw27), based on the locations of the first ATG codons downstream of the 150 bp sequence (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 3 show the classification and locations of ATG codons.

claims.claim: The 150 bp sequence is a hallmark of 'poison-and-antidote' genes that can potentially generate both poison and antidote isoforms.
claims.source: We propose that this 150 bp sequence is a hallmark of the 'poison-and-antidote' genes that can, at least potentially, generate both poison and antidote isoforms according to the dual-transcript model proposed by Nuckolls et al.
claims.evidence: This is a proposal based on the association of the 150 bp sequence with known dual-transcript killers and its position relative to alternative start codons.

claims.claim: Most wtf genes lacking the 150 bp sequence are 'antidote-only' genes.
claims.source: In addition, except for the eight most divergent genes (wtf7, cw7, wtf11, cw11, wtf14, cw14, wtf15, and cw15), they do not have an in-frame ATG codon in intron one or in the 5'-section of exon 2, suggesting that most of these genes are not able to generate a shorter isoform according to the dual-transcript model, and are thus 'antidote-only' genes.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from sequence analysis showing the absence of alternative in-frame ATG codons.

claims.claim: Nine wtf genes in the reference genome appear to have suffered pseudogenizing mutations.
claims.source: Our analysis of the gene structures of the 57 wtf genes in the reference genome and the CBS5557 genome showed that in addition to these five genes, four other wtf genes in the reference genome (wtf6, wtf8, wtf12, and wtf17), and three wtf genes in the CBS5557 genome (cw3, cw12, and cw16), appear to have suffered pseudogenizing mutations (see Materials and methods and Figure 5—source data 2), which include loss of start codons (wtf3 and cw3), premature stop codons (wtf1, wtf12, cw12, and cw16), frameshifting indels (wtf6, wtf8, wtf22, and wtf24), and segmental deletions (wtf2 and wtf17).
claims.evidence: This is based on gene structure analysis detailed in Materials and methods and Figure 5—source data 2.

claims.claim: Most wtf genes are predicted to contain either 5 or 6 exons.
claims.source: Most of the wtf genes in the reference genome and the CBS5557 genome are predicted to contain either 5 or 6 exons.
claims.evidence: This is based on gene structure predictions shown in Figure 5—source data 2.

claims.claim: The 6-exon genes clustered together in the DNA sequence-based phylogenetic tree.
claims.source: Interestingly, the 6-exon genes, including cw9, cw27, and all but one of the other ten 150-bp-sequence-containing genes, clustered together in the DNA sequence-based phylogenetic tree (Figure 5C), and their protein products are predicted to be longer and contain two or three more transmembrane helices than the protein products of 5-exon genes (Figure 5—source data 3, Figure 5—figure supplement 4, and Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: Figure 5C shows the phylogenetic clustering of 6-exon genes.

claims.claim: Protein products of 6-exon genes are predicted to contain two or three more transmembrane helices than protein products of 5-exon genes.
claims.source: Interestingly, the 6-exon genes, including cw9, cw27, and all but one of the other ten 150-bp-sequence-containing genes, clustered together in the DNA sequence-based phylogenetic tree (Figure 5C), and their protein products are predicted to be longer and contain two or three more transmembrane helices than the protein products of 5-exon genes (Figure 5—source data 3, Figure 5—figure supplement 4, and Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 4 and 5 show transmembrane helix predictions for different wtf protein products.

claims.claim: For each of the 12 150-bp-sequence-containing genes, the antidote protein product is approximately 50 amino acids longer than the poison protein product at the N-terminal soluble region.
claims.source: For each of the 12 150-bp-sequence-containing genes, the antidote protein product is approximately 50 amino acids longer than the poison protein product at the N-terminal soluble region.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the positions of alternative start codons shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The 10 C-terminal amino acids missing from the Td forms are strongly conserved among predicted protein products of 6-exon genes.

results.result: Two spore killer genes, cw9 and cw27, belonging to the wtf gene family were identified in the CBS5557 strain of S. pombe through NGS-assisted bulk segregant analysis and genetic deletion experiments. Both genes cause transmission distortion when present, with deletion of cw9 reducing segregation distortion and deletion of cw27 completely abolishing it in backcrossed strains.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C26 provide converging genetic evidence from bulk segregant analysis (Figure 1A-C) showing transmission distortion on chromosome III, which is reduced or abolished upon deletion of cw9 or cw27. The experimental design includes appropriate controls (backcrossed strains) and the statistical significance of transmission bias is demonstrated. The identification is well-supported by multiple independent lines of evidence.

results.result: The spore killers cw9 and cw27 act in a strain-background-independent and genome-location-independent manner, causing spore killing when integrated at various genomic locations (his3, lys1, leu1) in laboratory strain backgrounds.
results.evaluation: Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 demonstrate that cw9 and cw27 cause significant spore viability loss regardless of their genomic location in laboratory strain crosses. The experiments test multiple integration sites with appropriate controls, and statistical significance is reported (p-values via Fisher's exact test). The sample sizes (n=160-328 spores) are adequate for the conclusions drawn.

results.result: Killer-affected spores fail to undergo proper maturation, as demonstrated by electron microscopy showing that at 18 hours post-sporulation, affected spores exhibit lower electron density cytoplasm, visible organelles, electron-lucent spore walls, and often non-spherical shapes in a 2:2 pattern within asci.
results.evaluation: Figure 3C provides direct ultrastructural evidence through electron microscopy at multiple time points (12h and 18h). The 2:2 pattern of spore morphology in cw27-containing cells is consistent with Mendelian segregation of the killer allele. The comparison to control cells at the same time points provides appropriate controls for the maturation phenotype.

results.result: Spores carrying one killer are protected from its own killing effect but not from the other killer, demonstrating killer-specific protection. Heterozygous deletion of cw9 or cw27 causes significant spore viability loss affecting primarily deletion-carrying spores, while homozygous deletions have no effect. When both killers are present in different parents, mutual killing occurs.
results.evaluation: Figure 2 and Figure 3B provide comprehensive tetrad analysis data demonstrating the protection and mutual killing phenotypes. The experiments include appropriate genetic controls (homozygous vs heterozygous deletions) and statistical analysis (Fisher's exact test, exact binomial test). The sample sizes are adequate (n=160-328 spores per cross) and the results show clear statistical significance (p-values ranging from 1.94E-7 to 2.63E-23).

results.result: The killing and protecting activities of wtf killers can be uncoupled by mutation. Truncation analysis reveals that intact C-termini are important for killing activity while upstream sequences are important for protecting activity. Td versions lacking the last 10 amino acids retain protecting activity but lose killing activity.
results.evaluation: Figure 4 provides systematic truncation analysis with multiple constructs (Ta, Tb, Tc, Td, Te) tested in crosses. The separation-of-function is clearly demonstrated by Td versions that protect but do not kill (Figure 4B). Statistical significance is reported for all comparisons. However, the mechanistic basis for this separation remains unclear and would benefit from molecular characterization of the protein products.

results.result: The numbers and sequences of wtf genes vary considerably between S. pombe isolates. The reference genome has 25 wtf genes at 20 locations while CBS5557 has 32 wtf genes at 23 locations. Six CBS5557 singleton wtf genes exhibit exceptionally high sequence diversity (<85% identity) from their reference genome counterparts, indicating that wtf genes have diverged at a much faster pace than average genes.
results.evaluation: Figure 5 and supplementary figures provide comprehensive genomic analysis based on PacBio sequencing. The comparison of wtf gene divergence (<85% identity for some genes) to genome-wide divergence (3.1 SNPs/kb) clearly demonstrates accelerated evolution. The phylogenetic analysis and sequence alignments support the conclusions about rapid divergence.

results.result: Three singleton wtf genes (cw26, cw27, cw28) appear to have been lost in the laboratory strain through LTR-mediated recombination, suggesting this is a common mode of wtf gene turnover. The wtf-LTR association promotes gene loss and is detrimental to long-term persistence of wtf genes.
results.evaluation: Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 provide sequence analysis showing evidence of LTR-mediated recombination at the breakpoint junctions. The identification of three independent instances of the same mechanism supports the claim that this is a common mode of turnover. However, the claim about detriment to long-term persistence is somewhat speculative as it's based on observation of loss events without direct evidence of fitness consequences.

results.result: Phylogenetic analysis reveals that only 11 of 16 phylogenetic neighbor pairs are syntenic, while 5 pairs consist of non-syntenic genes, suggesting ectopic gene conversion contributes to inter-isolate differences. Genes within the same cluster are highly distinct from each other, possibly due to diversifying selection preventing sequence homogenization.
results.evaluation: Figure 5C shows the phylogenetic tree with appropriate bootstrap support values (≥95%) for defining neighbor pairs. The pattern of non-syntenic phylogenetic neighbors is consistent with ectopic gene conversion, supported by citations to similar phenomena in other gene families. However, the claim about diversifying selection (C52) is speculative and lacks direct evidence. The phylogenetic analysis appears sound but would benefit from additional tests for selection.

results.result: Twelve wtf genes (including cw9 and cw27) share a 150 bp conserved sequence in predicted intron 1, closely upstream of the transcription start site of a shorter wtf23 transcript isoform. These genes can be classified as Intron-1-ATG or Exon-2-ATG genes based on the location of the first ATG codon downstream of the 150 bp sequence. This sequence is proposed as a hallmark of 'poison-and-antidote' genes that can potentially generate both poison and antidote isoforms.
results.evaluation: Figure 5—figure supplement 3 shows the sequence alignment and relationship to the wtf23 transcript start site identified by Iso-Seq. The classification into two subtypes is clearly demonstrated. However, the proposal that this is a hallmark of poison-and-antidote genes (C70) is somewhat speculative, based on association with known dual-transcript killers rather than direct experimental evidence. The claim about 'antidote-only' genes (C71) is an inference from the absence of alternative ATG codons.

results.result: Introducing a 2.23 Mb pericentric inversion on chromosome I into the laboratory strain increased spore viability in crosses with CBS5557 from 14% to 22%.
results.evaluation: Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1 provide tetrad analysis data with appropriate sample sizes (n=240 and n=236 tetrads). Statistical significance is demonstrated (p=0.042, Fisher's exact test). This result establishes that chromosomal rearrangements contribute to but do not fully explain hybrid sterility, motivating the search for additional factors.

results.result: cw9 and cw27 share a nearly identical 288-bp-long conserved_up sequence upstream of their predicted start codons, which is also conserved upstream of many other wtf genes.
results.evaluation: Figure 4—figure supplement 1 shows sequence alignment demonstrating the conserved_up sequence. This is supported by citation to previous work (Bowen et al., 2003) that identified this conserved element. The sequence conservation is clearly demonstrated and forms the basis for subsequent truncation analysis.

results.result: Gene structure analysis reveals that 12 wtf genes appear to have suffered pseudogenizing mutations. Most wtf genes are predicted to contain either 5 or 6 exons, with 6-exon genes clustering together phylogenetically and encoding proteins with 2-3 more transmembrane helices than 5-exon gene products.
results.evaluation: Figure 5—source data 2 and 3, and Figure 5—figure supplements 4 and 5 provide comprehensive gene structure predictions and protein structure analysis. The AUGUSTUS predictions are described with appropriate parameter settings. The phylogenetic clustering of 6-exon genes (Figure 5C) and transmembrane helix predictions support the structural distinctions. However, these are computational predictions that would benefit from experimental validation.

results.result: For the 12 genes containing the 150 bp sequence, the antidote protein product is approximately 50 amino acids longer than the poison product at the N-terminal region. The 10 C-terminal amino acids missing from Td forms are strongly conserved among 6-exon genes, indicating Td-like mutations do not occur naturally.
results.evaluation: These claims are inferred from sequence analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and 4. The conservation of C-terminal amino acids is clearly demonstrated in the alignment. The inference about natural occurrence of Td-like mutations is reasonable based on the strong conservation, though it remains an inference rather than direct observation.

results.result: wtf genes contribute to extensive intraspecific reproductive isolation in S. pombe and represent ideal models for understanding how segregation-distorting elements act and evolve.
results.evaluation: This is a proposal based on the observation that different isolates have different sets of wtf killers causing mutual killing, combined with known severe hybrid sterility in S. pombe. While the mutual killing between cw9 and cw27 is well-demonstrated, the claim about contribution to reproductive isolation requires testing with additional natural isolates and quantification of the relative contribution of wtf genes versus other factors (like chromosomal rearrangements). The claim about being ideal models is subjective.

results.result: The wtf gene family has 25 members in the reference genome and is the largest species-specific gene family in S. pombe.
results.evaluation: The count of 25 wtf genes is supported by Figure 5 and citation to previous work (Bowen et al., 2003). The claim about being the largest species-specific family is supported by citation to Lespinet et al., 2002. These are well-established facts in the literature.

results.result: Most wtf genes locate on chromosome III, the smallest fission yeast chromosome and the only chromosome that tolerates disomy (occurring at >1% frequency during normal meiosis). The tolerance of chromosome III disomy may be advantageous to wtf gene family expansion on this chromosome.
results.evaluation: Figure 5A clearly shows the chromosomal distribution bias toward chromosome III. The facts about chromosome III disomy are supported by citations (Niwa et al., 2006; Molnar et al., 1995). However, the proposed connection between disomy tolerance and wtf gene expansion (C85) is speculative without mechanistic evidence or direct testing of this hypothesis.

results.result: The minimal sizes of fully functional cw9 and cw27 are both around 1.9 kb, and this compactness along with self-sufficiency likely has been advantageous to wtf gene family size expansion.
results.evaluation: The size estimate is based on truncation analysis (Figure 4) showing that Ta versions of approximately 1.9 kb retain full killing and protecting activities. However, the claim about advantage to family expansion is speculative, though reasonable. The connection between compactness and evolutionary success is plausible but not directly tested.

results.result: Background claims about meiotic drivers, gamete killers in other organisms, S. pombe natural isolate characteristics, and wtf gene evolutionary origin and distribution are established from prior literature.
results.evaluation: These claims are supported by appropriate citations to published literature and represent established knowledge in the field. They provide necessary context for the current work but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: wtf killers share features with Spok killers (single coding sequence, self-sufficient action) but encode multi-transmembrane proteins. A concurrent study by Nuckolls et al. showed wtf4 acts via a dual-transcript mechanism with poison and antidote isoforms.
results.evaluation: The comparison to Spok killers is supported by the functional characterization in this study and citations. The transmembrane protein prediction is shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 4 and 5. The citation to Nuckolls et al., 2017 is appropriate for the dual-transcript model, which provides a mechanistic framework for interpreting the truncation analysis results.

results.result: wtf genes were named for their association with Tf retrotransposon LTRs, but the presence of introns and lack of LTR sequence similarity indicate wtf genes have not been retrotransposed. The wtf-LTR association may reflect exploitation of wtf genes by Tf retrotransposons for insertion targeting.
results.evaluation: These claims are supported by citations to previous work (Wood et al., 2002; Bowen et al., 2003) and the structural features of wtf genes demonstrated in this study. The hypothesis about Tf exploitation (C80) is from cited literature and remains speculative but plausible.
